You will create a {C.HYPERTABLE} from scratch, see why time-based partitioning matters, and finish with queries you can reuse. Expect the same SQL surface you already know, with {C.CHUNK}-aware planning underneath.

## What is a {C.HYPERTABLE}?

A {C.HYPERTABLE} is the main abstraction {C.TIMESCALE_DB} uses for time-series data. To your application it looks and behaves like a regular {C.PG} table: you `INSERT`, `SELECT`, `UPDATE`, and `DELETE` using standard SQL. Under the hood, the database automatically partitions your rows by time into storage units called {C.CHUNK}s. Each {C.CHUNK} holds a time range of data (for example, one day or one week). When you run a query, {C.TIMESCALE_DB} figures out which {C.CHUNK}s are relevant and only touches those, instead of scanning the whole table. That is why {C.HYPERTABLE}s can scale to very large volumes while keeping queries fast.

For a deeper look at structure, partitioning, and indexes, see [Understand {C.HYPERTABLE}s](/learn/hypertables/understand-hypertables).

## Why use {C.HYPERTABLE}s?

Time-series data (sensors, metrics, events, logs) usually grows quickly and is queried by time range. A normal table can become slow and hard to manage as it gets large. {C.HYPERTABLE_CAP}s are built for that workload: they give you automatic time-based partitioning, efficient time-range queries, and scalable data management (for example, compression and retention) without changing how you write SQL. You get the familiarity of a {C.PG} table with the performance and scalability of a purpose-built time-series store.

## Advantages of {C.HYPERTABLE}s

- Efficient data management: Data is split into {C.CHUNK}s by time. You can [tune {C.CHUNK} intervals](/build/performance-optimization/improve-hypertable-performance#optimize-hypertable-chunk-intervals) to match how you ingest and query (for example, one {C.CHUNK} per day or per week).
- Better performance: A time-descending index is created by default; you can add more indexes (including [unique indexes](/build/performance-optimization/hypertables-and-unique-indexes)) as needed. Queries use these indexes and only open relevant {C.CHUNK}s.
- {C.CHUNK_SKIPPING_CAP}: The planner skips {C.CHUNK}s that don't match your query (for example, a time filter), which [reduces work and speeds up queries](/build/performance-optimization/improve-hypertable-performance#enable-chunk-skipping).
- Advanced analysis: {C.HYPERFUNC_CAP} and related features let you aggregate and analyze large amounts of time-series data efficiently. See [About {C.TIMESCALE_DB} {C.HYPERFUNC}](/learn/hyperfunctions/about-hyperfunctions).
- Familiar interface: You interact with a {C.HYPERTABLE} exactly like a normal table; partitioning and optimization are handled for you.

## How are {C.HYPERTABLE}s used?

You use a {C.HYPERTABLE} like any other table: connect with your usual client, run `INSERT` and `SELECT` (and `UPDATE`/`DELETE` where needed). Typical use cases include:

- IoT and sensors: Device readings with a timestamp (temperature, humidity, location).
- Metrics and monitoring: Server or app metrics (CPU, latency, errors) over time.
- Events and logs: User or system events with a time component.

For creating, altering, and managing {C.HYPERTABLE}s in real projects, see [Understand {C.HYPERTABLE}s](/learn/hypertables/understand-hypertables). For issues such as unique indexes, compression, or dropping {C.CHUNK}s, see [Troubleshoot {C.HYPERTABLE}s](/build/tips-and-tricks/troubleshoot-hypertables).

## Make your first {C.HYPERTABLE}

You will create a simple {C.HYPERTABLE} for sensor-style data: a `conditions` table with time, location, device, temperature, and humidity. When you run the command, the table is created and automatically set up as a {C.HYPERTABLE} partitioned by the time column.

<Prerequisites context="procedure">
<PrereqCloudOrSelf />

- Your [connection details](/integrate/find-connection-details).
- Any client that can run SQL ({C.CONSOLE}, `psql`, or your app's SQL driver).
</Prerequisites>

<NumberedList>

<NumberedItem title={`Create the ${C.HYPERTABLE}`}>
Run the following SQL. The important part is the `WITH (tsdb.hypertable, ...)` clause: it tells the database to treat this table as a {C.HYPERTABLE}. The first column with a timestamp type (`time`) is used as the partitioning column by default. We use `tsdb.segmentby = 'device'` so that rows are grouped by `device` inside {C.CHUNK}s, which helps both query and compression when you filter by device. We use `tsdb.orderby = 'time DESC'` so that recent data is stored in an order that matches typical time-range queries.

```sql
CREATE TABLE conditions (
   time        TIMESTAMPTZ       NOT NULL,
   location    TEXT              NOT NULL,
   device      TEXT              NOT NULL,
   temperature DOUBLE PRECISION  NULL,
   humidity    DOUBLE PRECISION  NULL
) WITH (
   tsdb.hypertable,
   tsdb.segmentby = 'device',
   tsdb.orderby = 'time DESC'
);
```

You should see a confirmation that the table was created (exact message depends on your client). The table is now a {C.HYPERTABLE}: new {C.CHUNK}s will be created automatically as you insert data into new time ranges.

</NumberedItem>

<NumberedItem title="Insert a few rows">
Insert some sample rows so we can query the {C.HYPERTABLE}:

```sql
INSERT INTO conditions (time, location, device, temperature, humidity)
VALUES
   (NOW() - INTERVAL '2 hours', 'office', 'sensor-1', 22.1, 45.0),
   (NOW() - INTERVAL '1 hour',  'office', 'sensor-1', 22.3, 44.8),
   (NOW(),                      'office', 'sensor-1', 22.2, 45.1);
```

</NumberedItem>

<NumberedItem title={`Query the ${C.HYPERTABLE}`}>
Query it like a normal table:

```sql
SELECT * FROM conditions ORDER BY time DESC;
```

You should see your three rows, with the most recent first. Notice that you didn't have to mention {C.CHUNK}s or partitioning, you just use standard SQL. The database routes the query to the right {C.CHUNK}(s) for you.

</NumberedItem>

</NumberedList>

You have built your first {C.HYPERTABLE} and used it for inserts and a time-ordered query. From here you can add more data, add indexes, or enable features like the {C.COLUMNSTORE}. The [Understand {C.HYPERTABLE}s](/learn/hypertables/understand-hypertables) guide and [{C.HYPERTABLE_CAP} operations](/learn/hypertables/optimize-data-in-hypertables) cover those next steps.
